clinicalPearls: Caused by the nematode Angiostrongylus costaricensis, endemic in Central and South America, acquired by ingesting infective larvae on vegetation or in slugs and snails contaminating food
Larvae migrate to the mesenteric arteries of the ileocaecal region, producing an eosinophilic inflammatory mass
Classically presents with right lower quadrant pain, fever, a palpable mass and marked eosinophilia, closely mimicking appendicitis
Complications include bowel ischaemia, obstruction and perforation, and the diagnosis is often made only on the surgical specimen
Humans are dead-end hosts, so eggs and larvae are not usually found in the stool, unlike many other helminths
There is no reliably effective anthelmintic regimen; management is largely supportive and surgical for complications, and anthelmintics may even worsen the inflammatory reaction
Prevention relies on washing vegetables thoroughly and avoiding contamination of food by slugs and snails
reference.pathophysiology: Angiostrongylus costaricensis is a nematode whose definitive hosts are rodents and whose intermediate hosts are slugs and snails. Humans acquire infection by ingesting third-stage larvae, either directly in a mollusc or on vegetation and food contaminated by mollusc slime. The larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and migrate to the mesenteric arterial branches supplying the ileocaecal region, where the adult worms lodge and lay eggs. Because humans are unnatural hosts, the eggs and larvae become trapped in the bowel wall rather than reaching the lumen, and they excite an intense eosinophilic and granulomatous vasculitis. This inflammatory reaction thickens the bowel wall, forms a tumour-like mass and can compromise the blood supply, leading to ischaemia, obstruction or perforation of the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix.
additionalDifferentials: Ileocaecal Crohn's disease or other inflammatory bowel disease
Caecal or colonic carcinoma presenting as a mass
Other causes of an eosinophilic mass or eosinophilic enteritis
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count demonstrating marked eosinophilia and leucocytosis
Cross-sectional imaging showing ileocaecal wall thickening or an inflammatory mass
Histopathology of resected bowel demonstrating eggs and worms with eosinophilic vasculitis
Inflammatory markers and assessment for obstruction or ischaemia
Colonoscopy with biopsy when malignancy or Crohn's disease is considered
redFlags: Signs of bowel ischaemia, obstruction or perforation requiring urgent surgery
reference.prognosis: Many cases resolve spontaneously as the worms die, but those with ischaemia, obstruction or perforation require surgery and can have significant morbidity; overall mortality is low with timely surgical management.
pitfalls: Expecting to find eggs or larvae in the stool, which are typically absent in this dead-end infection
Assuming anthelmintic therapy is beneficial when it may aggravate the inflammatory response
Mistaking the inflammatory mass for malignancy or Crohn's disease
Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient from an endemic area with eosinophilia and an appendicitis-like picture
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Supportive management with observation, as many cases resolve spontaneously as the worms die
Surgical resection of affected bowel for ischaemia, obstruction or perforation, the mainstay for complicated disease
Avoid anthelmintic therapy, as there is no reliable regimen and drug-induced larval death may intensify the inflammatory reaction
Analgesia, fluid support and monitoring for evolving obstruction or ischaemia
Histopathological confirmation on the resected specimen, since eggs and larvae are not found in stool
Preventive advice on washing vegetables and avoiding ingestion of slugs, snails or their slime on food
